messages:
Soojin Lee: We need to decide this week: for the first public case study(s), do we publish *exact* metrics (e.g. “p95 820ms -> 410ms”, “$18 -> $11 / 1M tokens”) or do we stick to *ranges* (“~40–55% lower p95”, “~25–35% lower cost”)?

Soojin Lee: Context: Northwind draft currently has exact numbers in the Results section + a footnote on measurement method. Legal flagged “exact” as higher risk if dashboards move / if customer disputes later.

Camila Reyes: +1, and Sales is already asking if they can quote numbers in outbound. If we go ranges, we need to make sure it still feels concrete.

Ethan Wallace: From a story/credibility POV, exact numbers read way better. Ranges can feel like marketing fluff unless we’re careful.

Tyler Benson: For tracking + reuse in decks, ranges are easier to standardize. Exact numbers become a maintenance issue (someone will ask “is this still true?” every quarter).

Markus Klein: Technical POV: exact numbers are risky because p95 varies by workload shape (prompt length mix, time of day, region). If we publish exact, we need VERY explicit “workload + window” language.

Simran Kaur: +1. Also depends on whether it’s end-to-end (app) latency vs model inference. We’ve seen customers mix those.

Soojin Lee: If we do ranges, can we still include “before vs after” but rounded? Like “~2x improvement” / “cut in half”?

Michael Grant: Legal lens: publishing *exact* metrics is doable but only with (1) customer sign-off in writing on the exact statement, (2) clear qualifier on measurement methodology + time window, (3) no guarantee language (“will”, “always”).

Michael Grant: The bigger risk is: if it’s a specific number, it can be construed as a claim Redwood is making broadly (especially if Sales uses it out of context). Ranges + qualifiers reduce that risk.

Sofia Mendes: Adding: some customers will only approve ranges because exact numbers can be considered “confidential performance info.” If we push exact, approval cycles slow down.

Camila Reyes: Helios already said they’ll only do ranges + anonymized phrasing. Northwind seems more open, but their VP Eng asked for a review window and “no screenshots of internal dashboards.”

Rachel Kim: CS perspective: we should not set precedent that every case study needs exact metrics. It will make future customers feel like they have to share more than they want.

Ethan Wallace: Counterpoint: If Northwind is willing, it’s a strong anchor story for Dedicated. We can make it clear the numbers are for *their* workload.

Soojin Lee: What if we do: exact numbers for 1 flagship (Northwind) + ranges for the rest?

Michael Grant: I’d prefer a single policy for the program. But if we do exception-based, we need explicit internal guidance on when exact is allowed + how Sales can use it.

Tyler Benson: +1. Otherwise it’ll turn into “every AE asks for exact” and we lose control.

Markus Klein: Another compromise: publish ranges in the public page, and keep exact numbers in an internal proof doc / sales-only one-pager (with customer permission).

Simran Kaur: That’s my vote. Public: ranges + methods. Sales: exact with “customer-approved” tag and expiration date.

Camila Reyes: I like that. Also aligns with “don’t overburden reference customers.” Public stays lighter.

Ethan Wallace: If public uses ranges, can we still include one “hard” number that’s stable? Like uptime / availability over a window?

Michael Grant: Uptime/availability is also tricky unless it’s contractual SLA or clearly “observed over X days.” But yes, a single stable metric can be okay if customer approves.

Soojin Lee: For copy: something like “Reduced p95 latency by ~40–50% (measured at the model endpoint, 30-day rolling window)” + “Lowered serving cost per 1M tokens by ~25–35% after enabling batching + prefix cache.”

Markus Klein: That’s good if we’re specific about “model endpoint” vs “user-perceived.” We should add a line like “results vary based on prompt length distribution and output tokens.”

Sofia Mendes: Please avoid “cut cost by X%” if we can’t specify what cost includes (compute only vs total platform). Better: “inference unit cost.”

Tyler Benson: Operational note: if we go with ranges publicly, we should standardize the ranges format across all stories so it doesn’t look like we’re hiding.

Rachel Kim: And a “metrics disclosure” badge/footnote: “Customer-approved ranges; exact figures available on request for qualified opportunities” (if customer allows).

Michael Grant: Careful with “available on request” — that’s still publication in some sense. Recommend “may be shared in private reference conversations when approved by customer.”

Soojin Lee: Got it. Action proposal:
1) Public case studies default to ranges + methodology qualifier + ‘results vary’ language.
2) Exact numbers only in internal sales enablement artifacts IF customer explicitly approves exact + context + timeframe.
3) Sales guidance: must use the approved snippet + not extrapolate.

Camila Reyes: Works for me. I’ll add this to the program overview + intake/approval process.

Ethan Wallace: I’ll update Northwind draft to ranges + keep the exact numbers in the internal metrics worksheet.

Michael Grant: Please route the updated language through me/Sofia before it goes to the customer. And include the qualifier about time window + what’s being measured.

Soojin Lee: :thumbsup: I’ll post a suggested “metrics disclaimer” paragraph in this channel today.

Simran Kaur: Also please tag me when you update the Results section — I want to sanity check that the ranges match what we can prove.

Tyler Benson: I’ll make a HubSpot field note: “Public metrics: ranges only” so we don’t accidentally copy/paste exact into outbound.

Camila Reyes: Perfect. Closing the loop here once Soojin drops the disclaimer copy.
